title: Healing at the Beautiful Gate
summary: Going up to the temple for afternoon prayer, Peter and John meet a man lame from birth who begs at the gate called Beautiful. Peter heals him in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, and the man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God. When a crowd gathers in Solomon's Colonnade, Peter explains that the power came not from the apostles but from the risen Jesus, and calls the people to repent and turn back to God.
story: Acts 2 ended with a summary: the apostles performed many wonders and signs, and the believers met daily in the temple courts. Chapter 3 zooms in on one such sign and the sermon it prompts. It is the first detailed miracle in Acts, and it shows the risen Jesus still healing through his followers exactly as he healed during his ministry. It also sets up the first conflict with the temple authorities in chapter 4. The healed man becomes living evidence that the name of Jesus carries power, and Peter's second sermon presses the people of Jerusalem to see their own Scriptures fulfilled in the one they rejected.
historical:
The temple in Jerusalem, rebuilt on a grand scale by Herod the Great from about 20 BC, dominated the city. Its outer court was surrounded by colonnades, long covered walkways lined with columns, and Solomon's Colonnade ran along the eastern side. It was a public meeting place, and Jesus himself had taught there (John 10:23). The early believers gathered there regularly (Acts 5:12). The gate called Beautiful is not named in other ancient sources, and its location is debated. Many scholars identify it with the Nicanor Gate, a magnificent bronze gate leading into the inner courts, while others place it on the eastern side of the outer court.

The ninth hour, about three in the afternoon, was the time of the evening offering in the temple, and many worshipers came to pray then. Peter and John, though now leaders of a movement proclaiming Jesus as Messiah, still keep the regular Jewish hours of prayer. The time frame is weeks or months after Pentecost, still in the early 30s AD.
cultural:
Giving alms (charity to the poor) was a major expression of piety in Judaism, and beggars sat at temple gates and city gates where worshipers passed. The man had been carried to the gate every day, apparently by family or friends, which suggests his begging was his only living. A man lame from birth, over forty years old (4:22), had no expectation of healing. He could see the temple courts but lived at their threshold.

Peter's speech draws on well-known titles and passages. The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob was how God named himself to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6, 15). Servant recalls the servant of the LORD in Isaiah, who is exalted and glorified after suffering (Isaiah 52:13-53:12). The prophet like Moses was promised in Deuteronomy 18:15-19, and Jews in the first century looked for such a figure. The promise that through Abraham's offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed draws on God's words to Abraham in Genesis 12:3 and 22:18.
literary: Luke pairs a miracle with a speech, a pattern he uses throughout Acts. The healing is told vividly, with a series of verbs (sprang, walk, walking and leaping and praising) that echo Isaiah 35:6, where the lame will leap like a deer in the time of God's salvation. Peter's speech moves from explanation (12-16) to accusation and offer (17-21) to Scripture and promise (22-26). It layers titles for Jesus: servant, Holy and Righteous One, Author of life, Christ, and prophet like Moses. The contrast in verse 14, a murderer released and the Author of life killed, is sharpened by the irony in verse 15. The speech ends not with condemnation but with blessing: God sent his servant first to Israel to bless them.

outline.t: The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
In the name of Jesus: walking, leaping, and praising God
Peter explains: not our power but Jesus' name
Repent and turn back: times of refreshing
The prophet like Moses and the promise to Abraham

doctrines.note: Peter calls his hearers to repent and turn back so that their sins may be wiped away. Repentance is more than regret; it is turning toward God, and it is met by forgiveness and times of refreshing from the Lord's presence. Peter even allows that they acted in ignorance, which leaves the door open.

Peter gathers Old Testament hopes around Jesus: the suffering Christ foretold by the prophets, the servant glorified by God, the prophet like Moses, and the offspring of Abraham through whom the nations are blessed. The Messiah had to suffer, which was the hardest point for Peter's hearers to accept.

The healing comes by faith in the name of Jesus. Peter is careful to deny any power or godliness of his own. Faith here is not a force the believer generates but trust that comes through Jesus and rests on him.

Heaven must receive Jesus until the restoration of all things. The Christian hope is not only personal salvation but the renewal of the whole creation that the prophets promised, which will come with Jesus' return.

words.note: Pais, which can mean child or servant. In verses 13 and 26 it means servant, and it echoes the servant of the LORD in Isaiah, whom the Greek Old Testament says God will glorify (Isaiah 52:13). The early church used this title for Jesus in its prayers (4:27, 30). It presents Jesus as the one who fulfills Israel's calling through obedient suffering.

Archegos, author, founder, leader, or pioneer: the one who goes first and opens the way for others. Author of life in verse 15 means the source and originator of life, and Peter sets it against the fact that the people killed him. The same word is used in Hebrews 2:10 and 12:2 for Jesus as the pioneer of salvation and faith.

Apokatastasis, restoration. Used only here in the New Testament. It speaks of God setting everything right, as the prophets promised. The disciples had asked about restoring the kingdom to Israel (1:6, using a related verb), and Peter now places that restoration within a larger renewal of all things at Jesus' return.

Epistrepho, to turn or turn back. Paired with repent in verse 19, it gives repentance a direction: turning to God. It is the Greek Old Testament's regular word for Israel returning to the LORD, and it echoes the prophets' calls to return.

christ: This chapter shows the risen Jesus at work through his apostles, doing what he did in his earthly ministry: making the lame walk. Peter insists that the name of Jesus, which stands for his person and authority, healed the man. The titles Peter uses reveal who Jesus is: God's servant who suffered and was glorified, the Holy and Righteous One whom they rejected, the Author of life whom they killed, the Christ whose suffering the prophets foretold, and the prophet like Moses whom all must hear. He now waits in heaven until the restoration of all things. The chapter's final word is that God raised up his servant and sent him first to Israel to bless them, turning them from their wickedness. The judgment Peter names is real, but the purpose he announces is blessing.

hard.q: Does the restoration of all things mean that everyone will finally be saved?
hard.a:
The word apokatastasis was later used by the third-century theologian Origen and others for the idea that all creatures, perhaps even the devil, will finally be restored to God. That view, often called universalism, has had defenders in the church's history and today, and they appeal to passages like this one and Colossians 1:20.

Most Christian traditions have not read Acts 3:21 that way. In context Peter speaks of the restoration that God announced through the prophets, which in the Old Testament includes both the renewal of creation and judgment on those who persist in evil. The very next verses warn that everyone who does not listen to the prophet like Moses will be completely cut off from among his people (3:23). Most interpreters therefore take the restoration of all things as the renewal of the world and the setting right of God's people, not the certain salvation of every individual. The passage offers hope and urgency together.

questions: The lame man expected money and received something far greater. When have you asked God for something small and found he had something else in mind?
Peter refused to take credit for the healing. Why is it so tempting for leaders and ministries to let people think the power is their own?
Peter told those who had rejected Jesus that God sent him to bless them. How does that shape the way you think about people who reject the gospel today?
